source.title: On damage of interpolation to adversarial robustness in regression

page_placements.theme: Adversarial risk can diverge from ordinary generalization

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Reports neural-network test prediction error across training epochs, using an empirical setting different from the claim’s original double-descent investigations. It does not sweep model size or measure ordinary test error across sample sizes for the relevant sample-size claim.
record.gate_note: The paper cites double-descent work in its background, but cited results are not this study’s results. Its numerical sample-size comparison measures adversarial prediction risk, not ordinary test error; those findings are recorded under fits_no_version. The epoch-wise standard prediction-error results are relevant to V2, but the text does not report a complete fall-rise-fall trajectory.
record.test_reason: The study reports standard test error across training epochs (up to 1000) for a fixed feedforward network on Auto MPG regression. This bears weakly on V2 in a new setting. The paper's focus is adversarial risk of interpolators; the epoch data are incidental and given only as two endpoints plus the epoch of minimum risk.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors prove that highly interpolating estimators are minimax-suboptimal under future input attacks, even though interpolation need not hurt standard risk. They describe a curse of sample size and a blessing of dimensionality for adversarial risk. Their network example shows adversarial risk rising much more than standard risk as training error falls, with robustness favouring earlier stopping.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes minimax adversarial risk for interpolating nonparametric regression estimators and provides empirical regression experiments; it does not use the original double-descent size, epoch, or sample-size risk-curve procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Adversarial risk varies with attack magnitude, interpolation degree, sample size, input dimension, and training epoch in the settings reported.

fits_no_version.finding: For the Auto MPG d=2 network, adversarial risk at r=0.1 more than doubles from epoch 30 to epoch 1000, and reaches its minimum earlier (epoch 20) than standard risk (epoch 30).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Continued training toward interpolation hurts adversarial risk more than standard risk, and the robust-optimal stopping time is earlier.

fits_no_version.finding: In Case 2 at r=0.1, increasing n from 80 to 300 raises SI adversarial loss (1.233 to 2.246) while LP adversarial risk falls (0.191 to 0.121).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For highly interpolating estimators under input attack, more data can hurt adversarial risk (curse of sample size).

record.problems: The ordinary test-risk epoch evidence is limited to a fixed architecture and dataset; the explicit numeric comparison gives only two epochs and does not establish the full curve shape. The sample-size comparison relevant to interpolation measures adversarial risk, not ordinary test error.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 plots additional simulation conditions and methods, but the text does not give their numerical results; the explicit numerical Case 2, r = 0.1 sample-size comparisons are retained in R4–R7. Figure 4's d = 2 standard-risk trajectory is represented by the explicitly reported endpoint comparison in R1; the d = 7 standard-risk curve is retained as figure-only in R3.

untested.parts: Relation to an interpolation threshold, label-noise or model-size dependence, and behaviour beyond 1000 epochs.
Ordinary test error versus sample size is not examined; the sample-size effects reported are for adversarial risk.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
No noise or regularization sweep of the double-descent peak.

missing.what: Epochs of minimum risk for d=2 (standard 30; adversarial r=0.05 and 0.1 both 20), and Figure 5 densities of the optimal epoch over 100 splits showing standard risk minimized later than adversarial risk.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not about double descent; it cites that literature only as background. The V2 link rests on an incidental epoch-wise standard-risk observation in one small tabular setting without label-noise manipulation, so the limits_scope label carries little weight. All sample-size and interpolation results concern adversarial L2-risk and do not bear on V3.

versions.untested_parts: Epoch-wise test prediction error is reported for a fixed neural-network architecture on Auto MPG; the paper does not establish a complete fall-rise-fall curve or test its relation to an interpolation threshold.
Sample-size comparisons concern adversarial prediction risk, not ordinary test error near an interpolation threshold.
No cross-model-class general double-descent curve is tested.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations.
The paper studies noise and interpolation in adversarial risk, not whether noise or regularization drives double-descent peaks, multiple peaks, or their disappearance.
No complexity recounting or conversion of a second descent into a U-shaped curve is tested.
